changes.before:
Most public plans rest on one picture of the future. A budget request, a staffing plan or a five-year goal usually assumes next year will look much like this one, only a little bigger or smaller. That works when conditions are steady. It works less well when the system itself changes, as it does when a workforce shrinks, a population ages or a funding stream ends. The Government Office for Science's Futures Toolkit draws the distinction this way: most forecasting models project past trends on a fixed view of how the system works, while futures thinking allows for change in the system itself. The further ahead you look, the wider the range of plausible futures becomes.

Foresight means preparing for several futures instead of betting on one. The U.S. Office of Personnel Management's foresight guide separates three kinds: the expected future, what we think will happen; alternative futures, what might happen instead; and the preferred future, what we want to happen. Holding all three in view keeps a plan honest and helps a leader tell a prediction from a hope. OPM says foresight complements a federal agency's required strategic planning rather than replacing it. The U.S. Government Accountability Office's Center for Strategic Foresight publishes trend papers that look five to 15 years ahead, a useful reminder that your own plan can look beyond one budget cycle.

Which future looks likely depends on where you stand. A leader's sense of the normal course of events is learned, and it is shaped by the people, data and communities that leader sees most often. If planning data counts only people who already use a service, the expected future quietly leaves out people who could not reach it. If a planning team shares one background or one work location, it may share the same blind spots. OPM's guide names cognitive bias directly and lists awareness of underlying assumptions among the benefits of foresight. Asking whose future a plan describes is an equity question and a quality question at once.

Foresight can start with one plan you already know. Minnesota Management and Budget's leader competency guide lists strategic thinking and vision setting among the skills expected of leaders of an organization, and this is one practical way to build them. Write down the future your plan assumes. Ask what would have to be true for it to arrive, what might happen instead, and who would feel the difference first. Bring the question to people who see the work from another position. Foresight supports better questions; it does not change what a law, rule or contract requires, and decisions stay with the areas responsible for them.

changes.before:
Horizon scanning, driver mapping and scenarios are three simple foresight tools. The Futures Toolkit groups its methods under three questions: what is changing, so what for our futures, and now what do we do. Each exercise starts with a scoping question that sets the topic and a time frame, often ten years or more. Horizon scanning gathers signs of change from many sources, including ones outside your usual field. OPM's foresight guide calls an early indicator of an issue that may matter later a weak signal. It offers scanning frameworks built on social, technological, economic, environmental and political factors, and advises including social factors in every scan.

Driver mapping sorts the changes you find by how important and how certain they are. A driver of change is a significant trend you can already observe that is expected to keep shaping the future. The toolkit places drivers on a grid along those two lines. Important and fairly certain drivers call for action now. Important but uncertain ones become the axes for scenarios: pick two, cross them, and describe the four worlds that result. A scenario is a plausible story, not a prediction. The toolkit suggests mixing hopeful and hard features in each world, then asking what three recommendations you would make if you lived there.

How a team imagines the future is a cultural practice. In a Minimization habit, the team assumes a change will reach everyone the same way and plans for a typical person. In an Acceptance habit, the team notices that the same driver lands differently, for example that online services help some people and shut others out, and that its own sense of the likely future reflects its vantage point. In an Adaptation habit, the team changes how the work is done: plain-language sessions, interpreters, accessible materials, and self-advocates, families and partners helping shape the scenarios. These describe routines, not people, and any team can move between them.

Involving the people affected is part of the method. The Futures Toolkit says diverse perspectives make futures work stronger and that participants should include people affected now and in the future. It also cautions that public participation takes time, that bias in choosing participants must be avoided, and that people should hear why their time matters and how their input will be used. Tell participants honestly what the exercise can and cannot change. If you plan to compensate community members or run a formal engagement process, check first with the responsible program area, which can tell you what applies.

changes.before:
A decision made today has to work in futures you cannot choose. The Futures Toolkit calls its method policy stress-testing, also known as wind tunneling. You take a policy, strategy or project and imagine it operating in each of several scenarios. For each one, you ask whether the option still works there, whether it no longer serves a purpose, or whether it needs to change. The rule is to stay inside the logic of each scenario and not adjust the scenario to rescue a favored option. A simple version fits on one page: list your options down the side and two to four scenarios across the top, and in each box write still works, no longer needed or needs change. Add a last row for each scenario: who would be most exposed here, and what second route would they have?

An option that works in every future can go forward, and one that works in only some can be changed or kept as a contingency plan. Options that work in none should be revised. The toolkit notes that a single workshop is rough and ready, and that the facilitator's challenge is to avoid groupthink or defensiveness about favored options. Asking people who did not design an option to help test it can make the conversation easier.

An equity analysis asks who is most exposed in each future. Exposure means who would be harmed first or most if conditions change, and who has the fewest alternatives. People who rely on one channel, one provider or one staff person are often more exposed than an average figure shows. So are people whose language, disability, income or location already makes access harder. For each scenario, ask who carries the burden, what evidence you have and whose experience is missing from it. Then ask people closest to the service, including front-line staff and partners, whether your picture matches theirs.

Options that keep choices open are often the most practical. Keeping a second route to a service, starting with a pilot, setting a review date or writing down which signal would trigger a change all let a plan adjust without starting over. The toolkit's backcasting method adds a useful sort: mark each step as in your control, partly in your control or outside it, then plan how to influence the steps you do not control. Testing a decision does not change who makes it. Legal questions go to counsel, and the responsible program area decides how a rule or service is carried out.
changes.after:

changes.before:
Stewardship asks what will remain when you move on. Many decisions a senior leader makes outlast the leader: a multi-year agreement, a redesigned service, a new way of paying partners. Each one carries the futures its authors assumed, often without saying so. When those people leave, the next team inherits the commitment but not always the reasoning, and may keep defending a plan whose conditions have quietly changed. Stewardship means leaving the next team able to test a decision, not only carry it out.

Knowledge transfer is one part of stewardship, and another course covers it in depth. OPM's 2022 Workforce Planning Guide asks leaders how they will transfer knowledge from experienced staff to entry and mid-career colleagues, and OPM's succession planning guidance names shadowing, communities of practice and action learning among its development methods. This lesson looks at something less often done: leaving the foresight behind a decision in place, so the people who come later can keep asking whether it still fits.

Leave the assumptions, signals and review dates with the decision. For each long-lived commitment, write down the future it assumes and the alternatives the team considered. Name the signals that would show conditions shifting, such as a change in the workforce, in who applies or in how people reach a service, and who would feel the shift first. Put review dates in a shared calendar, not in your memory, and say what each review should ask. Keep this with the official records, follow your area's records practices, and keep it about the work, never about individual people.

Culture outlasts a leader only when it lives in routines. A habit of asking who is missing, testing decisions against several futures or reviewing results with partners will fade if it depends on one person's reminder. Build one such question into a standing agenda, a decision template or a regular review so it runs without you. Before you go, ask what happened under your leadership, for whom, and what the team should keep, change or stop. Stewardship is about functions and knowledge; who fills a position is decided through hiring with Human Resources.

after.title: U.S. Office of Personnel Management: Succession Planning Process (2005)
after.note: Supports the mention of communities of practice, shadowing and action learning as development methods in lesson 4. Federal guidance from 2005, used for concepts only; knowledge transfer is taught in depth elsewhere.

after.title: Minnesota Management and Budget: Enterprise Leader Competency Definition Guide
after.note: Supports that Minnesota's leader competency guide lists strategic thinking and vision setting among skills for leaders of an organization. It sets expectations and does not teach foresight methods.

after.title: IDI — Resources and Intercultural Development Continuum
after.note: Defines orientations toward cultural difference; the course examples do not assess individuals or teams.

after.title: DHS — Equity Policy
after.note: Required agency equity analysis and learning are not waived by an optional improvement exercise.

after.title: Minnesota Statutes 13.05 — Duties of responsible authority
after.note: Data collection, use and disclosure duties apply to mapping and analysis; removing names does not automatically make information public.

changes.reason: Clarify forecasting and scenario limits, authorized participation, access safeguards, records and timely action.

sourceChecks.source: UK Government Office for Science, Futures Toolkit, August 2024
sourceChecks.evidence: Primary OGL guide: forecasting can vary assumptions; driver mapping, four scenarios, participation, stress-testing and backcasting. A single workshop is provisional, not proof that an option is safe or authorized.
24-page primary PDF: expected, alternative and preferred futures, weak signals and drivers, cognitive bias and social factors. Federal planning guidance rather than Minnesota authority.
Primary page confirms its role and five-to-fifteen-year trend-paper horizon.
Five-page primary guide, page 4 lists action learning, communities of practice and shadowing. Concepts retained without importing federal staffing practices.

sourceChecks.source: MMB Enterprise Leader Competency Definition Guide, March 2024
sourceChecks.evidence: Primary 20-page PDF, page 12 lists strategic thinking and vision setting under Leading the Organization.

sourceChecks.source: IDI resources, DHS Equity Policy and Minnesota Statutes 13.05
sourceChecks.evidence: Primary sources distinguish assessed orientations from examples, required agency equity analysis from optional tools, and authorized data handling from blanket omission of individual facts.
